imperial.name: Capsicum

actions.text:
Sow indoors

Chillies Feb–Mar. Outdoor sweet peppers late Mar–early Apr.

Plant out

Apr–May under warm glass. May–Jun outdoors after frost.

methods.text:
Sow indoors 

Sow two seeds per pot and keep the stronger seedling. Sweet peppers need 65–70°F to germinate and chillies about 70°F. Buy young plants if you cannot supply steady warmth.

Pot on 

Move seedlings gently into larger pots as roots fill their pots. Keep them warm and bright.

Plant out 

Harden off for an outdoor crop. Wait for warm nights, set at pot depth and water in. A cloche gives shelter while plants settle.

text:
Capsicum.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Sweet peppers and chillies are colourful, heat-loving relatives of tomatoes and potatoes. Perennials in their native climate, they are tender annuals in Britain, most reliable under glass or in warm shelter. Green peppers are edible but immature. Ripening changes their colour and, in many varieties, makes them sweeter or hotter with deeper flavour. Fully coloured fruit take longer and slow new fruit production: choose between an earlier, heavier green crop and fewer, later ripe peppers.

Quick facts
Sow indoors

Chillies Feb–Mar. Outdoor sweet peppers late Mar–early Apr.

Harvest

Aug – Oct

Germination

14–21 days

Planting depth

Set at the same level as in the pot.

Row spacing

18 in. between rows

Yield per plant

6-10 fruits

Plant spacing

Between plants: 18 in.; compact varieties 12 in.

Ready in

About 18 weeks from sowing

Plant out

Apr–May under warm glass. May–Jun outdoors after frost.

Recommended varieties
Redskin

Compact sweet pepper for pots or small greenhouses; green fruit ripens red.

California Wonder

Familiar blocky sweet pepper. Pick green or ripen red in warm protection.

Corno di Toro Rosso

Long, tapering, thin-skinned red sweet peppers for cooking; an alternative to bells.

Demon Red

Compact chilli for pots, with small, hot fruit. Give warmth and shelter.

Habanero Orange

Very hot orange chilli needing a long, warm growing season.

Key risks
Poor fruit set

Flowers may fail to set during cold, excessive heat or drought.

Red spider mite

Sweet peppers can develop pale mottling and bronzing when red spider mites feed beneath leaves.

Blossom end rot

Brown patches appear at the bottom of the fruit - a frequent problem where growing bags are used.

Slugs

Slugs may damage young plants and late, slow-ripening fruit near the soil surface.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
34
FRUITING CROPS

Give young plants reliable warmth.

Under cover is the most dependable UK route, especially in cooler areas.

Choose green or ripe-coloured harvests.

Early picking encourages more fruit; full colour usually gives deeper flavour.

Sowing & planting
Raise in warmth
Set the final plant
Sow indoors 

Sow two seeds per pot and keep the stronger seedling. Sweet peppers need 65–70°F to germinate and chillies about 70°F. Buy young plants if you cannot supply steady warmth.

Pot on 

Move seedlings gently into larger pots as roots fill their pots. Keep them warm and bright.

Plant out 

Harden off for an outdoor crop. Wait for warm nights, set at pot depth and water in. A cloche gives shelter while plants settle.

Soil & preparation
Fertile, moist, drained soil or peat-free compost. Warmth and shelter; avoid cold, wet roots.
Use pots, growbags or greenhouse beds; outdoors needs warm shelter.
Looking after the crop
Water evenly and mulch. Keep fruit dry and ventilate hot houses without chilling young plants.
Feed with organic potash feed as fruit swells. Stake heavy stems. Inspect leaf undersides for mites and use biological control early. Dampen hot greenhouse floors and ventilate.
Harvesting & storage
Pick glossy green fruit for earlier, heavier yields; leave to mature colour for fuller flavour. Ripening adds 2–4 weeks and usually reduces new fruit.
Cut with a short stalk. Dry only sound, fully ripe chillies in warm, airy conditions. Discard mouldy fruit.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Poor fruit set	Flowers fail to set, especially in cold.	Maintain warmth; avoid drought, overheating and cold checks.
Red spider mite	Pale mottling, bronzing; mites beneath leaves.	Identify early; use suitable predatory mites under cover.
Blossom end rot	Brown sunken patch at fruit base.	Keep root moisture even; avoid dry growing bags.
Slugs	Seedlings or low fruit are chewed.	Inspect and hand-pick; support fruit clear of soil.
Aphid	Colonies on tender shoots and leaves.	Squash damaging colonies and encourage natural predators.
Whitefly	Small white flies; sticky or sooty leaves.	Inspect new plants; use suitable biological control under cover.
Grey mould	Grey fluffy mould on damaged tissue.	Remove infected tissue; ventilate and avoid wet fruit.
Anthracnose	Dark, sunken lesions on fruit or foliage.	Remove affected material; keep fruit dry and seek diagnosis.
Cutworm	Young plants are severed at the base.	Use seedling collars; inspect nearby soil.
Final tips

Regularly picking some green peppers frees the plant to set more fruit.

Use gloves when handling hot chillies and avoid touching your eyes.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
35
FRUITING CROPS
